entries.title: Bulls overwhelmed by Boston as the defense remains an ongoing issue
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON – There are flashes with this Bulls group.</p><p>Moments where the front office can say, ‘OK, we have something there.” Just not a lot, and even less Monday night in Boston.</p><p>Much like the young Bulls (1-3) looked like in Toronto in the season opener last week, it was a roster that just couldn’t compete but for a few minutes here and there with the Celtics, evident in the 134-99 one-sided defeat.</p><p>That was on display by the third quarter when a 12-point halftime deficit turned into a laugher, as the home team outscored the Bulls 39-21 in the stanza thanks to 19 points from sharp-shooter Payton Pritchard.</p><p>But it’s not like Boston just outlasted the Bulls from outside. They outscored them in the paint 46-30 and outrebounded them 54-40, including grabbing 19 offensive rebounds.</p><p>That’s what irked coach Tiago Splitter the most on a list of disappointments in the loss.</p><p>“We knew that was a very good team shooting the three-ball, but when you give them second and third chances it’s impossible,” Splitter said. “The biggest reason (for the loss) is we’ve got to rebound the ball better, we’ve got to take care of the ball, and shoot the ball better as well.”</p><p>Pretty much the entire gambit needed to improve.</p><p>And while his players were in full agreement, the defensive side of the ball – included the rebounding – was expected to be better. That’s what has been the most disappointing for Matas Buzelis; he expected more.</p><p>“We can be really good defensively,” Buzelis said. “Just thinking me, Caleb, Stix, (Nic) Claxton, Lenny (Miller), we’re all really athletic, long, so we have all the tools. It’s just the process of getting that understanding of what position we’re in, how to attack the offense, how to get back … it’s like telepathic, honestly. Sometimes you can’t explain basketball. Something happens and you know where to be at.</p><p>“Like I knew last year I could be really, really aggressive being low man with Isaac (Okoro) because he would scramble so you knew where to go, so it takes some time.”</p><p></p><p><b>Nic of time</b></p><p></p><p>The Bulls could have used a certain 6-foot-11 athletic big to help deal with Mitchell Robinson and Neemias Queta in the game against the Celtics, and Nic Claxton (hamstring) continued moving closer to answering that bell on Monday morning.</p><p>“He’s getting better,” Splitter said of Claxton. “(Monday morning) he did a good workout on the court, not with the team yet. We’re looking to increase those practice, individual workouts at the start of next week and hopefully get him with the group soon.”</p><p>The Celtics offered up the latest evidence on the Bulls’ lack of size, beating up the visiting team 30-19 on the glass in the first half. That was coming off a loss to the Wizards in which the Bulls were outrebounded 48-44.</p><p></p><p><b>Fix the hitch</b></p><p></p><p>Miller has proven to be an efficient scorer overall, but the Bulls feel there’s an entirely different gear for him in becoming an improved three-point shooter.</p><p>Miller has a hitch in his shot and the coaching staff is working on making that a bit more smoother for the forward.</p><p>“It’s not something that is easy to change, especially when you have that habit,” Splitter said. “But just trying to get smoother and make him feel comfortable. At the end of the day, you gotta make shots. It doesn’t matter how it looks, right? We’re putting a lot of effort into all the guys and shooting. It’s part of the development with this team that everybody becomes a better shooter.”</p><p>Miller entered the Celtics game shooting 23.1% from three in a small sample size this season but shot 35.6% in 27 games with the Bulls last year.</p>

entries.title: Man shot during argument in West Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A man has been hospitalized after he was shot during an argument in West Englewood Monday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 38, was arguing with another man in the street in the 2000 block of West 68th Place at 5:30 p.m. when the other man shot him in his leg and abdomen, police said. The wounded man was taken to Christ Medical Center in serious condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: A forgettable start for the Bulls' Matas Buzelis as he finds his way
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON — It’s easy to forget that Bulls forward Matas Buzelis has a 40-point game on his résumé. Forty-one points, actually, on a 16-for-28 shooting night against the Warriors in March.</p><p>It’s easier to forget that during that same month, in his second NBA season, he averaged 20.7 points, 7.1 rebounds and 1.8 blocks over 14 games.</p><p>Is this season starting the way he’d like it to? Not even close. But the notion he’s somehow regressing or isn’t a true foundational piece in the Bulls’ latest rebuild left him shaking his head with a laugh Monday.</p><p>“We have Norm [Powell], Caleb [Wilson], both ultra-aggressive, so you’ve got to figure out the right time to shoot,” Buzelis said before the Bulls (1-3) fell hard in a 134-99 loss to the Celtics at TD Garden. “Not just me — all of us. That’s why we all watched film together [Sunday], players only, trying to figure out how things need to work.</p><p>“Once we figure out our spots, where we want to go, and then everyone figures out what they’re going to shoot, the shots they’re going to take, it will be easier to understand the game. Right now, how we’re shooting is like freestyle. We really don’t know what we have to get into or what sets we have to be aggressive in. But I know this group is very passionate about basketball and what we have to do to get there, how we can compete every night, [to] be the best team we can be.”</p><p>How does Buzelis (11 points Monday) see himself fitting into the equation specifically?</p><p>“What do people think — you’re going to come in and get buckets right away?” he said. “It’s a process. I’ve been working really hard, worked hard this summer, so all I need to really do is get out there and trust my skills. I’m still trying to figure out where I can hunt my shots at, where I can be aggressive. And once that happens, we’ll be just fine, all of us.”</p><p>“All of us” is a focal point for him this season: Getting together for extra film sessions. Talking it out. Getting on the same page.</p><p>That cohesiveness also falls on first-year Bulls coach Tiago Splitter. It’s great that Wilson, the No. 4 overall draft pick, dropped 30 points on the Wizards in his first home game Saturday — but it came in a loss. Splitter knows Wilson is a huge piece in what the Bulls hope to achieve, but he’s not the only one. His philosophy is making sure Buzelis and Wilson develop at the same time.</p><p>“Play the right basketball,” Splitter said. “Coach them, teach them. Be on it when it’s needed. I think that’s how you build a team — you build winners.</p><p>“I don’t think there’s any secret there. It’s not just ‘Let them play.’ You have to coach them where to be, how to do it. . . . It’s a balance, also, where you play random basketball and sometimes you call a play for one of those guys. So, it’s a balance for sure.”</p><p>Buzelis is on board — he just wants to make sure he’s on the floor to help make it happen. That wasn’t the case last Friday night, when he was benched for the entire fourth quarter of the Bulls’ victory over the Bucks.</p><p>“If we see [forward] Lenny [Miller] is playing better than me, creating more advantages, you play him,” Buzelis said. “As a competitor, of course I’m a little annoyed, I want to be out there. But I also have a responsibility to show that I belong out there, that I belong on the court at the end of a game. That’s on me to play hard, create problems for the opposing team. That’s my responsibility.”</p>

entries.title: Feds say Quincy man mailed letters containing white powder to members of Illinois congressional delegation
entries.summary: <p>A 36-year-old Quincy man is accused of mailing letters containing white powder to four members of Congress from Illinois, including a senator and three House members, according to a criminal complaint filed in the U.S. District Court Monday.</p><p>Matthew Unglesbee faces charges of mailing threatening communications, false information and hoaxes, according to the complaint filed in the Central District of Illinois.</p><p>The letters contained a white granular substance and handwritten messages, including “HA HA” and “HAH enjoy the gift,” according to an FBI affidavit. Preliminary testing did not detect chemical or biological toxins in the substance.</p><p>During an interview with FBI agents Sunday, Unglesbee allegedly admitted mailing the four letters. He told investigators the substance was salt and said he used it because it resembled anthrax, according to the affidavit. Unglesbee said he knew the powder would be taken seriously and would have “hazmat come in white suits.” He claimed he was joking, but acknowledged recipients could perceive the letters as dangerous.</p><p>The letters were postmarked in Springfield on Oct. 19. While searching Unglesbee's home, investigators also found an empty, unmailed envelope addressed to a congressional office in Washington, D.C.</p><p>The complaint does not identify the four congressional recipients by name. Several <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/16/schneider-quigleys-offices-receive-suspicious-letters-amid-pre-election-threats" >Illinois lawmakers have publicly reported receiving suspicious mail</a> in recent weeks, including Democratic Reps. Mike Quigley, Brad Schneider and Jan Schakowsky. Quigley and Schakowsky each reported another letter last week.</p><p>Sen. Tammy Duckworth's office also confirmed receiving two suspicious letters in the mail in recent weeks. The letters were mailed to Duckworth's Chicago office.</p><p>It has not been confirmed that all of those incidents are connected to the case against Unglesbee, though in a statement to the Sun-Times, Quigley said he was “relieved to learn” an arrest had been made in connection with one of two suspicious mailings sent to his Chicago office.</p><p>“This individual, and whoever is responsible for the other suspicious mail received around the country, must be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” Quigley said in a statement. He also thanked the Chicago Fire Department’s hazardous materials unit for responding to both incidents.</p><p>Schakowsky released a statement Monday afternoon saying she was aware of reports of someone being arrested in connection with the letter sent to her Skokie office last week. She also expressed gratitude to the law enforcement officers "who acted quickly and decisively to help ensure the safety of me and my staff and are working to hold those responsible accountable."</p><p>Schneider’s office issued a statement last Wednesday saying it had received another piece of suspicious mail at his Lincolnshire office. Schneider thanked law enforcement agencies for their response and investigation, according to his office’s public statement.</p><p>The investigation continues.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/21/2-chicago-area-members-of-congress-receive-another-suspicious-package" >2 Chicago area members of Congress again received ‘suspicious’ packages</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Friend suggests I buy pricey gifts for her kids, then lists the items for sale
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I are friendly with another couple, "Matt" and "Mara." They have two young children, one of whom is autistic. We have five children, so we understand the daily challenges of parenting.</p><p>My husband and Matt have been friends since preschool. I met Mara soon after she and Matt started dating. We weren't that close until after we both had children. When it comes time for birthday and Christmas gifts, Mara and I always ask each other what our kids would like for a gift. Besides the usual toys, books, etc., Mara always asks for expensive sensory items for her autistic son.</p><p>I adore her son, but I roll my eyes every time she sends me a link for a $90 memory foam chair. My husband doesn't see a problem. We just buy more things for their other child so they are treated equally.</p><p>My problem is that within a few months, I see Mara has listed my gift for sale online. It hasn't happened just once, but multiple times — pajamas with the tags still on, a $50 plastic climbing dome and an expensive race car track that Mara specifically asked me for.</p><p>When I brought it up to my husband, he was a little peeved at first. After it happened again, he brushed it off, saying that maybe Mara had asked multiple people for the same gift and ended up with two of the same thing.</p><p>I could understand if she had used the gifts for a while and then her kids weren't interested anymore, but the fact that her ad says these items were brand-new and never used seems like a slap in the face. Do I have a right to be upset? Should I just stick to gift cards from now on? — <i>GENEROUS FRIEND IN THE EAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR FRIEND:</b> Could Mara be doing this because she needs the money? Of course you have a right to be upset about the wasted effort that went into purchasing these gifts. You might feel less peeved if you were to give her gift cards to spend on her children, but there's no guarantee that's how they'd be used.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> At a recent wake service, I hugged the wife of the deceased and told her how sorry I was for her loss. She thanked me for coming, and I responded, "I wouldn't have missed this." Later, I wondered if that sounded flip, like putting my attendance on the same plane as not missing a concert or sports event. What might have been a better response to her thanking me? Or was that acceptable? — <i>WANTING TO BE RESPECTFUL</i></p><p><b>DEAR RESPECTFUL:</b> Wakes, visitations and funerals are emotional events. We're all prone to minor gaffes and other social awkwardness under such circumstances. I'm sure the widow understands you meant no disrespect. In the future, you might phrase that sentiment more like this: "It was important to me to be here for you." You can also never go wrong by paying a simple, heartfelt compliment to the deceased.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Illinois is focused on facilitating — not limiting — voter access
entries.summary: <p>Since taking office, the Trump administration has attempted to assert federal executive control over our nation’s elections. This has led my office, in partnership with other state attorneys general across the country, to file <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/07/attorneys-general-state-officials-sue-over-trump-admins-2nd-attempt-to-cut-permanent-housing-funds" >lawsuits</a> challenging the administration’s unlawful actions and has generated news headlines that range from confusing to alarming.</p><p>No doubt many Illinoisans are experiencing uncertainty and possibly even apprehension around casting their votes in the general election. However, I encourage you to tune out the noise, and if you have not already, make your plan to vote today.</p><p>Here’s what you need to know.</p><p>The Constitution gives states the responsibility of administering elections. Voters can have confidence that our elections are safe and secure and can rest assured that in Illinois, we are focused on facilitating, not limiting, your access to the ballot box. Illinoisans have several options to cast votes, including by mail, in-person early voting and going to the polls on Election Day.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-370000" name="module-370000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>A recent U.S. Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/14/supreme-court-rejects-trump-mail-ballot-restrictions-midterm-elections" >decision</a> secured by my office and other state attorneys general ensures that voting-by-mail operations will proceed as usual, without any federal restrictions.</p><p>The last day to request a mail-in ballot is Thursday. Illinois voters can vote by mail for any reason, and you can request a mail-in ballot through your local election authority. You can look up your local election authority using the <a class="Link" href="https://www.elections.il.gov/ElectionOperations/ElectionAuthorities.aspx" target="_blank" >Illinois State Board of Elections</a> website.</p><p>Ballots can be returned by mail, to the local election authority or, in many jurisdictions, a secure drop box. If possible, return your ballot to your local election authority or a drop box, where available. You can check the Illinois State Board of Elections website for a <a class="Link" href="https://www.elections.il.gov/VotingAndRegistrationSystems/VoteByMailBallotDropBoxLocations.aspx?MID=0RRSrGzAdpc%3d&T=638023004082804731" target="_blank" >list of drop box locations</a>.</p><p>If you return your ballot by mail, do so as early as you can to make sure it is received on time. Ballots must be postmarked by midnight Election Day. The U.S. Postal Service recommends mailing ballots at least one week before the deadline for submitting them. If you take your ballot to a Postal Service retail location on or near Election Day, request a manual postmark at the counter. Mail-in ballots cannot be accepted at polling places or early voting locations.</p><p>Early in-person voting has begun in many areas in Illinois and will continue until the day before Election Day. You can find out about early voting in your area by visiting the Illinois State Board of Elections website.</p><p>If you opt to vote in person on the Nov. 3 Election Day, polling places are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. You are entitled to cast a ballot as long as you are in line at the time the polling place is scheduled to close.</p><p>Voters do not need to show an ID to vote. A poll worker should not ask you for ID, except in a narrow range of circumstances. Only voters who are registering on Election Day, need to change their registration address, or registered to vote by mail without providing an ID need to present ID at the polls.</p><p>If you are eligible to vote but not registered, you can still register at the office of your local election authority under the <a class="Link" href="https://www.elections.il.gov/VotingAndRegistrationSystems/EarlyVotingLocationsSearch.aspx" target="_blank" >guidelines of grace period registration</a>.</p><p>It has been the longstanding practice of the attorney general’s office to monitor elections in Illinois to ensure that voters’ rights are protected and polling places are accessible. Voting no longer takes place only on Election Day, so my office has expanded its monitoring efforts. Teams of attorneys from my office are in the field monitoring polling places around Illinois now and on Election Day.</p><p>We also rely on voters to report issues that they observe. If you encounter activity that you suspect could be illegal, contact my office by calling 866-536-3496 in Chicago and northern Illinois or 866-559-6812 in central and southern Illinois. Our hotlines are open now and will remain open through Nov. 17.</p><p>Voters can find more information about their rights and options for voting by visiting the <a class="Link" href="https://ilagaction.quorum.us/voterinfo2026/" target="_blank" >election resource hub</a> on my office’s website. The attorney general’s office is also sharing information for voters through our social media accounts.</p><p>No matter who you vote for, you have a right to cast your ballot freely and fairly. It is incumbent upon each voter to set aside any distractions and invest in our country’s future by exercising that sacred right. Knowing your rights and making a voting plan will ensure that your vote will be counted.</p><p><i>Kwame Raoul is Illinois’ attorney general.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7a0000" name="module-7a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Ballot measure asks if Chicago needs permanent festival site
entries.summary: <p>A measure on this November’s ballot asks Chicago voters if they’d like the city to establish a designated, permanent spot for large-scale festivals and events.</p><p>It is one of several non-binding questions this election cycle, and it arrives after pushback in recent years from some Chicagoans who oppose privately run festivals taking place in the city’s public spaces, from Lollapalooza in Grant Park to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2024/09/19/neighbors-riot-fest-douglass-park-traffic-crowds-music" target="_blank" ><u>Riot Fest in Douglass Park</u></a>.</p><p>The measure, introduced by 11th Ward Ald. Nicole Lee, will gauge public interest in Chicago designating a location for such festival-sized events. However, the measure itself is light on details and doesn’t come with clear next steps. The wording simply asks: Should Chicago develop a permanent festival and outdoor event space for large-scale events?</p><p>Some advocacy groups are urging voters to pass the referendum, envisioning a Some residents in the surrounding neighborhood have complained the festival damages the park’s green space.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>This year, both <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lollapalooza/2026/08/03/heres-what-grant-park-looks-like-after-lollapalooza-clears-the-stages" target="_blank" ><u>Lollapalooza</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/09/21/riot-fest-cleanup-douglass-park-mud" target="_blank" ><u>Riot Fest</u></a> were held during rainy weekends, which led to muddy conditions on the ground. While those festival organizers are required to pay to repair the fields where the events take place, the conditions also raised concerns among attendees with disabilities.</p><p>Supporters of the Chicago measure point to Milwaukee as a framework. A post on the <a class="Link" href="https://www.reddit.com/r/chicagoEDM/comments/1x62ad5/vote_yes_on_the_chicago_permanent_festival_space/?solution=5af32e061679be085af32e061679be08&js_challenge=1&jsc_token=2824be10929bdc604753c70a67a1c331bf9a9391d303f98dd5b6d3f56916fb8b&jsc_orig_r=" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago EDM subreddit</u></a> called on followers to vote in favor of the proposal, saying, “A dedicated festival space like this will just elevate the Chicago festival experience for everybody. Permanent stages will ensure the most optimal setup for every fest, and dedicated bathrooms, as opposed to porta potties, will make the events that much nicer for us.”</p><p>In Milwaukee, the annual Summerfest is held on designated festival grounds, which are owned by the city and operated by a nonprofit. Throughout the year, the space also hosts a variety of other concerts and festivals.</p><p>How cities operate their outdoor music venues has been the subject of recent scrutiny. The <a class="Link" href="https://cdn.vanderbilt.edu/vu-URL/wp-content/uploads/sites/412/2026/09/17174438/How-State-and-Local-Governments-Pay-for-Live-Nations-Monopoly.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Vanderbilt University study</u></a> found that half of Live Nation’s amphitheaters are publicly owned by a city or state, including Chicago’s Huntington Bank Pavilion on Northerly Island. The study’s authors argue those arrangements are disproportionately favorable to Live Nation by forgoing competitive bidding, offering below-market rent, and giving the corporation the chance to sell naming rights for publicly owned venues.</p><p>In total, the report found that at least $420 million in taxpayer money nationwide has gone to benefit Live Nation, the multinational corporation, which operates venues, owns Ticketmaster and manages artists. In April, a Manhattan jury found that <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/04/15/nx-s1-5786715/live-nation-ticketmaster-antitrust-verdict-monopoly" target="_blank" ><u>Live Nation acted as a monopoly</u></a> and unfairly controlled too many aspects of the live entertainment industry.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-510000" name="image-510000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f31478e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2386x1339+57+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2F33%2F15196bcd4c808df9115803b76035%2Fap060629026562.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1fc4fdc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2386x1339+57+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2F33%2F15196bcd4c808df9115803b76035%2Fap060629026562.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/11bb66b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2386x1339+57+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2F33%2F15196bcd4c808df9115803b76035%2Fap060629026562.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="People arrive for the opening day of Summerfest Thursday, June 29, 2006, in Milwaukee. The city's festival grounds lost power Thursday during the opening day of Summerfest in an incident that sent a man to the hospital, police said. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/11bb66b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2386x1339+57+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2F33%2F15196bcd4c808df9115803b76035%2Fap060629026562.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fa48ccd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2386x1339+57+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2F33%2F15196bcd4c808df9115803b76035%2Fap060629026562.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/11bb66b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2386x1339+57+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff2%2F33%2F15196bcd4c808df9115803b76035%2Fap060629026562.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Some advocacy groups envision a city resource similar to Milwaukee’s Summerfest grounds, which that city owns and is operated year-round through a nonprofit. Here, people arrive for the 2006 opening day of Summerfest.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>AP Photo/Morry Gash</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Brian Shearer, the lead author of the Vanderbilt study, advocates for cities to either operate their own venues — like Red Rocks Park and Amphitheatre, which is owned and operated by the city of Denver — or use the “outsourcing with conditions” model. The latter would include a competitive bidding process, charging market-rate rent, and allowing all artists, regardless of management, to appear. Oftentimes, Live Nation only books the artists on its management roster to play these venues, the study notes.</p><p>“Cities should include in the contracts an insistence on making sure that the public is protected,” Shearer said. “Don't let the venue operator charge excessive fees to residents. Don't let the venue operator only have the venue open to the artists that they promote. We think these are sort of basic public protection terms that cities could be including in their contracts.”</p><p>In Chicago, it’s not clear what the next steps would be if residents support the ballot initiative. The measure also does not specify if the city would both own and operate the outdoor event space, or if it would contract it out.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: IHSA football playoff takeaways: CCL domination, long-term benefits of expansion
entries.summary: <p>It is nearly impossible to get through a postgame interview with a Catholic League football coach without mentioning how strong the conference is and how well it prepares teams for the postseason.</p><p>That is true, and the results were obvious in the opening round of the Illinois High School Association’s state football playoffs. The Catholic League went 12-1,, and its only loss was one of the weekend's closest games: Benet’s 42-38 defeat to Moline.</p><p>Marist, St. Patrick, DePaul Prep, St. Laurence, Notre Dame, Carmel, Nazareth, Joliet Catholic, St. Francis, Providence, Marmion and Leo all won in the opening round.</p><p>DePaul Prep, St. Laurence and Carmel won just three games during the regular season and would not have qualified for the playoffs under the old format. Nazareth won just four games, but probably would have snuck in on playoff points.</p><p>“Playing the schedule we played in the Catholic League really prepared us for the playoffs,” Notre Dame coach Dan DeFranza said. “We all notice that a lot of Catholic schools do well in the playoffs. It’s because we beat the crap out of each other in the regular season and every week is a real focused game plan. It is the regular season that prepares us for the playoffs, for sure.”</p><h3>Another benefit of playoff expansion</h3><p>So, Catholic League schools clearly believe a tough schedule is key to improving your team and winning the playoffs. That's likely another benefit of playoff expansion. Now that above-average (but not dominant) teams no longer have to worry about winning five games to make the playoffs, they can schedule more challenging nonconference games, raise their schedule difficulty, and be better prepared for the playoffs.</p><p>In the past, it wouldn’t make much sense for your average Mid-Suburban League team to risk facing Lincoln-Way East or Loyola in Week 1. But under the new format, that may benefit the team.</p><h3>Round review</h3><p>Home advantage was key in the opening round: 92 of 128 host teams won (72%). The median margin of victory was 28.5 points. But the average opening-round score was 41-13. There were many blowouts, but not more than the first round of the previous format.</p><p>However, overanalyzing the opening-round results isn't the point. Many of the teams playing were in their first playoff game in decades. One hope for the expanded playoffs is that many significantly below-average teams can use playoff experience, extra practices, and renewed hope throughout the season to build better programs over the next few years.</p><p>One athletic director told me this weekend that students at his school used to be embarrassed to be on the football team. This season’s playoff run changed that; it literally impacted the mood in the hallways. That is a monumental shift, something only possible because of the playoff expansion. It may take a few years for that to pay off, which is why this past weekend's scores aren't significant.</p>

entries.title: Last mayoral candidates file signatures for 2027 ballot
entries.summary: <p>Fifteen candidates will vie for the right to deny <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-announcement-reelection-bid-2027" >Brandon Johnson</a> a second term and become Chicago’s 58th mayor, but only if they can survive cutthroat petition challenges that could narrow the field considerably.</p><p>Joining the mayoral field on the final day of filing were: retiring Illinois Comptroller Susana Mendoza with a self-reported 26,000 signatures; cardiologist and political newcomer Lisa Nee with what she says are 31,000 signatures; Cook County Board of Review Commissioner George Cardenas with a self-reported 31,500 signatures; and Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas with what she said is "slightly shy of" 40,000 signatures.</p><p>Also joining the mayoral field on the final day of filing were attorney William Quinlan, businessman Joe Holberg, conservative Danielle Carter-Walters, former real estate developer Zoe Ma, John Kitover and Jessica Maronto.</p><p>Five candidates filed their nominating petitions on the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/19/mayor-race-candidates-stacks-nominating-petitions-chicago-board-of-elections" > first day of filing:</a> Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias; lobbyist John Kelly; former Chicago Housing Authority Chair Matthew Brewer; U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley and millionaire businessman and perennial political candidate Willie Wilson.</p><p>That brings the total number of mayoral candidates to 16 — but that is likely to change.</p><p>Campaign managers and veteran political operatives said they expect the crowded mayoral field to shrink substantially as candidates closely scrutinize each other's nominating petitions to make certain they have the required 12,500 valid signatures to remain on the ballot.</p><p>No one will be immune from those challenges no matter how it looks, or whom it might knock off the ballot. That includes Johnson, who skipped opening day, and therefore, the lottery for the top spot on the ballot. He said he filed 33,000 signatures Friday.</p><p>That’s a relatively low number for an incumbent mayor. Richard M. Daley, Chicago’s longest-serving mayor, once filed more than 100,000 signatures with the help of the once-powerful Democratic ward organizations filled with city workers.</p><p>“I’m looking at everybody — particularly the African American ones,” Wilson told the Chicago Sun-Times. “And if somebody do challenge me, I’m very confident that we’re OK. But that’s up to them if they want to spend the money.”</p><p>Asked whether he believes Johnson will have a problem making the ballot, Wilson said, “He’s the mayor. He’s been through this before. He ought to have his stuff in order, I would think."</p><p>The challenge period begins Tuesday and ends Nov. 2. The adjudication of challenges will continue until Dec. 17, when the final mayoral ballot if certified.</p><p>“I know for a fact that different people have pulled Dr. Wilson’s petitions and are going through them line-to-line," said former state Sen. Ricky Hendon, who is handling petition challenges for Wilson. "The only thing I can guarantee is they can’t get him because we did the work, went down to the Board of Elections and verified the signatures before we filed them. Some campaigns did not do that."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fb0000" Alice Palmer off the ballot.</p><p>“Everybody has to do the work to get on the ballot. If you don’t have the signatures, that’s a problem. … That’s why they have the challenge process. Everyone is gonna be held to that scrutiny," Jubeh said.</p><p>Veteran political operative Victor Reyes, advising the Nee campaign, expects Giannoulias to concentrate his challenges on Quigley and others with the greatest potential to draw votes along the “vote-rich” north lakefront.</p><p>That’s where Johnson sealed his 2023 mayoral victory, and where the 2027 election is expected to be decided once again.</p><p>“You do everything you can to structure the race regardless of how they beat you up” for being the big-bucks candidate who “compromises democracy,” said Reyes.</p><p>Kelly is likely to challenge Mendoza, who is targeting the same conservative voters in Northwest and Southwest Side wards that are home to scores of police officers and firefighters. And Mendoza is likely to challenge Cardenas, the only other Hispanic in the race.</p><p>Giannoulias could challenge Kelly and Mendoza, as well as Pappas, a fellow Greek-American with whom he has a long-standing rivalry. </p><p>"He’s going for a first-round win and, with all of that money, he has the resources and the ability" to narrow the field enough to improve his chances, Reyes said.</p><p>Pappas filed her petitions wearing a shirt reading, "No biceps, just brains," a veiled jab at Giannoulias that she said "speaks for itself."</p><p>That was a reference to what she told the Sun-Times about Giannoulias the day candidates began circulating nominating petitions. “If you want to be mayor of the city of Chicago, your IQ has to be higher than your body temperature. … That’s what’s going to be required in the mayor’s race."</p><p>Pappas and Cardenas were among six candidates filing within an hour of the deadline on Monday, thereby entering a lottery for the coveted last spot on the ballot. The others were Holberg, who said he gathered 32,000 signatures; Carter-Walters, who said she had 13,000 signatures; Ma with a self-reported 17,000 signatures, and Maronto.</p>

entries.title: The Soul Train Awards are coming 'home' to Chicago for the first time
entries.summary: <p>For the first time in its nearly 40-year history, the Soul Train Awards ceremony is coming home to Chicago.</p><p>Presented in partnership with the city, the event will take place at the Harris Theater for Music and Dance on Nov. 5 and air on BET and CBS at 8 p.m. EST (7 p.m. CST) on Nov. 27. Actor Anthony Anderson will serve as host, and Chicago superstar <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/16/chaka-khan-chakzilla-sia-west-end-musical-chicago-music" >Chaka Khan</a> will receive the Classic Soul Honor.</p><p>Though Don Cornelius launched the iconic “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/8/17/23836328/love-peace-and-soul-train" >Soul Train</a>” TV show in Chicago in 1971, the awards spinoff has taped in other cities, including Los Angeles, Atlanta, New York and Las Vegas, since its inception in 1987.</p><p>“Chicago is where the ‘Soul Train’ story began, and bringing the awards back to my hometown is a full-circle moment,” BET President Louis Carr said in a release. “‘Soul Train’ helped shape how the world experienced Black music and culture.”</p><p>In a statement, Mayor Brandon Johnson championed Chicago as a city of “Black creativity and innovation.”</p><p>“Bringing the ‘Soul Train Awards’ back to its hometown is an opportunity to celebrate that legacy while creating new opportunities for local artists and entertainment professionals, supporting our small businesses and strengthening Chicago’s creative economy,” he said.</p><p>Airing until 2006, “Soul Train” became known for its slate of legendary Black performers, influential dancers and iconic “Soul Train" line. </p><p>A continuation of the brand, the Soul Train Awards are returning after a two-year hiatus. For this ceremony, producers have embraced a <a class="Link" href="https://www.billboard.com/music/awards/soul-train-awards-return-bet-air-date-1236325496/" target="_blank" >new format</a>, which honors music icons, includes new fan voting categories and features a partnership with Spotify. Performers and other awards recipients will be announced at a later date.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/09/16/chaka-khan-chakzilla-sia-west-end-musical-chicago-music" >2026 is the year of Chaka Khan, from her new album with Sia to a West End musical</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Gun still drawn when cops get to scene, FBI agent fatally shoots Chicago man in Pilsen
entries.summary: <p>When Chicago police arrived at the scene in Pilsen Monday night, an FBI still had his gun drawn, pointed at a 27-year-old man lying on the sidewalk with multiple gunshot wounds Monday evening in Pilsen.</p><p>Chicago police were called to the 1700 block of South Union Avenue around 5:30 p.m. Monday and found the FBI agent with his gun drawn on a 27-year-old man lying on the sidewalk, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times. A handgun lay underneath a bicycle, which was nearby in the street, according to the report.</p><p>The 41-year-old agent was standing next to a black Nissan with flashing red and blue lights, according to the report.</p><p>The 27-year-old, of the Near West Side, suffered gunshot wounds to both legs, the chest and the right flank, according to the report.</p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital where he was pronounced dead at 6:24 p.m., according to police and the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>In a statement, the FBI said it was reviewing the agent-involved shooting. </p><p>"The FBI takes all shooting incidents involving our agents or task force members seriously," the statement said. "In accordance with FBI policy, the shooting incident is under review by the FBI’s Inspection Division."</p>

entries.title: Agente del FBI mata a hombre en Pilsen; aún tenía el arma en mano cuando llegó la policía
entries.summary: <p>Cuando la Policía de Chicago llegó a la escena en Pilsen la noche del lunes, un agente del FBI todavía tenía su arma desenfundada y la apuntaba a un hombre de 27 años que yacía en la acera con múltiples heridas de bala.</p><p>La policía de Chicago acudió a la cuadra 1700 al sur de Union Avenue alrededor de las 5:30 p.m. el lunes y encontró al agente del FBI apuntándole al hombre de 27 años, según un informe policial obtenido por el Sun-Times. Según el informe, una pistola estaba debajo de una bicicleta que se encontraba cerca de la calle.</p><p>El agente, de 41 años, estaba junto a un Nissan negro con luces rojas y azules intermitentes, según el informe.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-300000" name="module-300000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El hombre de 27 años, residente del área, sufrió heridas de bala en ambas piernas, el pecho y el flanco derecho, según el informe.</p><p>Fue llevado al Hospital Stroger, donde fue declarado muerto a las 6:24 p.m., según la policía y la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>En un comunicado, el FBI dijo que estaba revisando el tiroteo en el que estuvo involucrado el agente. "El FBI se toma en serio todos los incidentes con disparos que involucren a nuestros agentes o a miembros de los grupos de trabajo", señaló el comunicado. "De acuerdo con la política del FBI, el incidente de disparo está siendo revisado por la División de Inspección del FBI".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Special Council meeting could blow $75 million hole in Mayor Johnson's budget
entries.summary: <p>Three City Council leaders who negotiated the compromise that sweetened Stonepeak Partners’ $2.53 billion deal to acquire Chicago's parking meters are calling a special City Council meeting Monday to take action that could blow a $75 million hole in Mayor Brandon Johnson’s tax-heavy budget.</p><p>Finance Chair and 3rd Ward Ald. Pat Dowell, her Finance predecesso,r Scott Waguespack (32nd), and Ald. Nicole Lee (11th) want to compel Johnson to use the $75 million up-front payment from Stonepeak they negotiated without the mayor’s help to be applied to the 2026 city budget as an extra payment that chips away at the city’s $36 billion pension crisis.</p><p>Without consulting the City Council, Johnson decided to use the $75 million windfall to help defray the cost of the $363 million pension advance for 2027. That’s not what the Council intended, nor was it what the ordinance that was passed by a 46-3 vote required.</p><p>That ordinance stated that the up-front payment that the city received when Stonepeak closed the deal last week — as well as profit sharing going forward — must be earmarked for pension payments over and above the $2.79 billion pension payment required by state law.</p><p>“Our goal was always to use this money to reduce our pension liability — not to maintain a steady level,” Dowell told the Chicago Sun-Times Tuesday.</p><p>“We have to start somewhere. … It’s a good use of the funds to reduce taxpayer liability for pensions. Every year, most of our property tax … goes toward pensions. This helps to reduce that liability for taxpayers. ... If we just wanted the money to be used any old way, we would have been silent on that in the ordinance we passed in September and allowed those dollars to go into the general fund.”</p><p>Lee added, “The earlier you can make credit card payments, the better off you are in the long run.”</p><p>If the City Council approves the ordinance, it would create a $75 million gap in Johnson's proposed $17.6 billion budget, which is already tenuously balanced with $480 million in borrowing to cover police settlements, and $664.2 million in new and increased taxes. Anti-administration alderpersons also have threatened to reject Johnson’s corporate head tax for a second straight year.</p><p>Asked how the $75 million gap would be filled, Dowell said, “That’s not my problem. “It’s on him to come up with the $75 million."</p><p>“Hopefully, this is a collaborative effort and we can figure this out together. But this is what happens when the communication breaks down,” Dowell said.</p><p>“He took the right from the Council to determine how the [up-front] payment would be allocated by just placing it in the budget the way he wanted to do it. He had nothing to do with [sweetening the parking meter deal]. And we were not given any indication except through the budget that his intent was to use this money in this manner. There was no conversation.”</p><p>Lee agreed that “the mayor’s got to figure out” how to plug the $75 million gap if the up-front payment from Stonepeak is not made available to be used toward next year’s pension advance.</p><p>“It’s clear in the legislation we passed for the parking meter deal that the City Council would decide that. We negotiated the transfer. That’s our purview. It’s our job,” Lee said. “This is just a pattern of his. We have not been super-engaged in the process on many things… I can’t say that I have a bad relationship with the mayor. But it’s not an ongoing dialogue.”</p><p>Last month, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/29/city-council-parking-meters-deal-compromise-stonepeak-partners" >Council gave final approval </a>to New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners’ $2.53 billion bid to acquire Chicago parking meters after a negotiating team led by Dowell, Lee and Waguespack brokered a compromise to sweeten the deal for the city. </p><p>It calls for the city to receive a $75 million transfer fee at closing, 5% of net income going forward and 2% of the sale price if and when the meters are sold again before the deal ends in 2084. The compromise also reduces costly compensation the city is required to pay for every space taken out of service.</p><p>Those “true-up payments” cost the city nearly $174 million through 2025.</p><p>Stonepeak also agreed to sell Omni Air International, an airline that has provided long-haul deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security during President Donald Trump’s deportation campaign. And the company agreed to explore creating entire non-metered city blocks as “potential electric vehicle charging stations with charging revenues shared with the city.”</p>

entries.title: Newly launched Northwestern Medicine Transplant Institute aims to lead way for transplant innovation
entries.summary: <p>Northwestern Medicine announced Tuesday the launch of the newly created Transplant Institute, which aims to lead the way in organ transplant innovation.</p><p>The Northwestern Medicine Transplant Institute, which so far has raised about $26 million in philanthropic funding, will bring together four of Northwestern’s existing programs, which include the Northwestern Medicine Organ Transplant Centers, the Northwestern Medicine Center for Transplant Innovation, Northwestern Medicine Center for Transplant Research and Education and the Northwestern Medicine Center for Transplant Access.</p><p>The institute includes a staff of about 300 people, ranging from social workers to nurses to surgeons. Last year, Northwestern Medicine performed 691 transplants, according to a news release.</p><p>“When hope is lost in anywhere across the globe, Northwestern comes to mind as a place that could potentially deliver that hope through innovative techniques,” said Dr. Satish Nadig, the institute’s executive director, adding that he wants the institute to become the destination for transplant innovation.</p><p>Northwestern transplant patients will notice more conversations about possible trials they could be eligible for as the institute also conducts research, Nadig said. For example, Northwestern is currently doing research to see if transplant patients can get off of anti-rejection medication, which organ recipients typically have to take for the rest of their lives.</p><p>The field of transplants dates back to the 1950s but has stagnated since around the 1990s, Nadig said. The institute will also see how technology, like artificial intelligence, could be used to match recipients and donors.</p><p>In Illinois, there were more than 4,700 people waiting for an organ transplant as of October, with the majority waiting for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/08/chicago-area-woman-finally-gifted-kidney-transplant-by-sun-times-reader-after-years-of-searching" target="_blank" ><u>kidney donor</u></a>, according to data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network. The new institute will include transplants for all organs and include pediatric transplants, Nadig said.</p><p>“All of these isolated things that challenge conventional boundaries, we make them mainstream,” Nadig said. “We make them more integrated into our everyday care so that we aren’t just doing transplant, which is a phenomenal thing, we’re actually changing the field of transplantation in a very deliberate manner.”</p><p>The launch of the Transplant Institute coincided with the six-week check up for Arthur Nichols who had a kidney transplant in September at Northwestern. Nichols, 70, of West Bloomfield Township, Michigan, decided to seek out a transplant at Northwestern after his family learned there was a doctor there who specialized in transplants for patients who had multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that damaged Nichols’ kidneys, he said.</p><p>Unknown to Nichols, his 42-year-old daughter, Natalie Nichols, of Fishers, Indiana, had undergone the process to see if she was a match and was selected as his kidney donor. The two underwent the procedure Sept. 18.</p><p>“If you had a chance to save your best friend, you would do it,” Natalie Nichols said. “And for me, my dad is my best friend so it was a no brainer. And even today, being able to spend time with him and just see his color and his energy, is just amazing.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> But now, she’s starting to see his energy return. entries.title: A new West Side mural park is set to open next summer

Ogden Ave. on the site of a former auto parts shop. The project is backed by individual donors and the suburban Vivo Foundation, founded by former Medline Industries president Andy Mills and his wife, Nancy.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" entries.title: Mayor Johnson steps up political attacks on billionaire businessman Michael Sacks
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson on Tuesday accused billionaire businessman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/16/michael-sacks-profile-chicago-billionaire-mayoral-race-brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-rahm-emanuel" >Michael Sacks</a> of leading a “nasty coalition of billionaires” who are using their wealth to elect school board members who would close more Chicago Public Schools.</p><p>Johnson never mentioned Sacks by name. But it was clear he was talking about Sacks, who has helped bankroll a political action committee known as Common Ground Collective that has raised more than $5 million to elect Jessica Biggs as school board president and other school board members who would not be beholden to the Chicago Teachers Union.</p><p>Common Ground has so far outspent the CTU by a more than three-to-one margin and is airing television commercials that target Hilario Dominguez, the union’s candidate for board president against Biggs.</p><p>“We’re seeing a really nasty coalition of billionaires who don’t send their children to public schools, but all of the sudden, they have a stake in our public education,” Johnson said.</p><p>“That one individual who whispered into the ear of a previous administration to shut down 150 schools. Keep in mind he only closed 50, of which 2,000 children are missing. Don’t even know where they are. Can you imagine how brutal and how cruel you have to be to shut down schools in communities where we’ve seen violence spike, where vacancy exists?</p><p>"That same individual who called for the closing of Black and Brown schools," Johnson continued "…is now spending millions of dollars to elect people who want to do more of the same." </p><p>In an interview this month for an in-depth Sun-Times profile of Sacks, CTU Vice President Jackson Potter accused Sacks of having “supported the mayor or stood silently at best” when then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel “closed the greatest number of schools in American history in 2013, almost exclusively in the Black community.”</p><p>Johnson’s broadside marked a dramatic escalation of that same line of attack — with a week to go before the election of the city's 21-member board of education and school board president.</p><p>Sacks responded to Johnson’s latest attack by flatly denying any role in Emanuel’s school closings.</p><p>“The Mayor's comments on school closures are false. I never advocated to close any schools and I don’t now. The comments are however ironic as I was in fact a major advocate for Treasurer [Kurt] Summers' Catalyst Fund from which BUILD [Building Up Independent Local Developers] is receiving money to make the very grants the Mayor announced today,” Sacks said in a statement.</p><p>“In addition I helped create and was a staunch supporter of the Neighborhood Opportunity Fund which rewrote the zoning code to favor disinvested neighborhoods over downtown. The Mayor knows all of this but he chooses to make things up which isn’t going to help him."</p><p>Sacks is scheduled to receive the Nostra Aetate Award Thursday night from the Archdiocese of Chicago to recognize his leadership in the Jewish community, and in promoting interfaith dialogue. The award has become a source of controversy among conservative Catholics because Sacks and his wife, Cari, have long supported women’s reproductive choice.</p><p>Earlier this week, Cardinal Blasé Cupich justified the decision to make Sacks the award's first recipient.</p><p>“We recognize that now more than ever we need to find ways to reinforce the special relationship between the Catholic community and the Jewish people,” Cupich said in a prepared statement. </p><p>“Honoring individuals who do not share core Catholic teachings recognizes their dignity, leadership role and service to their community without implying an endorsement of every statement or stance they maintain” and that “dialogue cannot occur if respect is contingent upon complete agreement on church doctrine or political policy,” Cupich's statement said.</p><p>Johnson was asked what he thought of the Archdiocese giving an award to “somebody who has become somewhat of a boogeyman” for his administration.</p><p>“I don’t believe in boogeymen or ghosts. I don’t. That’s quite childish, to be quite frank with you. What I do believe in is investing in people, and I believe that those that have means have a moral responsibility to contribute more," Johnson said. “I do see people as a means of creating a fair and a just society. That’s the hope that I bring. And I believe that the people of Chicago are better off when there is an equitable distribution of wealth.”</p><p>Sacks has contributed millions of dollars to Common Ground, an advocacy organization that also has a PAC and a super-PAC that has spent millions to advocate for and against school board candidates and support moderate City Council members who have opposed Johnson.</p><p></p><p>“The way that this individual is spending — we do know the outcome that manifests as a result of his vision for Black and Brown communities… Now, that would be monstrous and scary. That is something to boogey away from,” Johnson said.</p><p>Sacks has been Johnson’s political pinata for well over a year now.</p><p>When a 31-member coalition of conservative and moderate City Council members rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax, the mayor blamed Sacks, though the commercials he bankrolled against elements of the mayor’s 2026 budget never mentioned the head tax. Those commercials attacked other major elements of the budget and poked holes in Johnson’s claim that he was increasing spending for violence prevention.</p><p>On the day<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-announcement-reelection-bid-2027" > Johnson launched his bid</a> for a second term, Johnson identified Sacks as his primary political opponent and attacked him repeatedly by name.</p><p>The escalation of the tension between Johnson and Sacks was triggered by a question during Tuesday's news conference that apparently hit a raw nerve with the mayor: Whether next Tuesday’s historic election for seats on the 21-member elected school board would “send a message about the strength of” the CTU and the now-fractured coalition of progressive unions that helped put Johnson in office.</p><p>Last week, the long-simmering feud between Johnson and that coalition boiled over, triggering a pivotal endorsement for Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias in the race for mayor.</p><p>“Labor is split all over the place — especially when it comes to this race,” Johnson said. “I’m not sure if there is a coalition that’s akin to mine, and one that I’ve been responsible to build.”<br></p>

entries.title: Alex Vlasic hasn't abandoned his Blackhawks playoff hopes: 'Nothing is out of the question'
entries.summary: <p>Alex Vlasic's goal of helping the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> finally make the playoffs this season is off to a rough start.</p><p>But a rough start is all it is, Vlasic mentioned Tuesday. Only a small portion of the season has been played, and he's not ready to give up on that goal yet.</p><p>"Because of the results we've been getting, it feels like it's worse than it is," Vlasic said. "We're 11 games into the season, so nothing is out of the question at all. We still think we have a team that's capable of playoffs, for sure. That's our goal."</p><p>The Hawks' 25-year-old longest-tenured defensemen wasn't shy to toss around the word "playoffs" in interviews over the summer, hoping to almost <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/08/23/blackhawks-alex-vlasic-playoffs-louis-crevier-bowen-byram-patrick-kane" >speak it into existence</a> by vocalizing confidence and setting high, specific expectations.</p><p>And it's understandable why he did so. Vlasic has experienced lots of losing throughout his NHL career to date — entering Tuesday, the Hawks had won only 83 of his first 271 games — and it's surely getting old. As he stated after last season, "We're not here to do this again."</p><p>Those 188 losses have taught Vlasic some things, though, about mentally handling failure without letting it ruin him. As long as the Hawks continue struggling, he can at least fall back on those psychological techniques to manage his own attitude.</p><p>"As I get older, I've become more mature in the way I approach the game," he said. "I'm trying to focus on what I can control: my own play, how I show up to the rink every day, [the ways I can] get better and improve. I want to bring that into the locker room and have everybody have that same mindset. </p><p>"Honestly, I'm lucky to still be playing hockey as my job. There's a lot worse things going on in the world right now. We have to look at it from that mindset: we're able to play a game for a living and have a lot of fun doing it. If that doesn't get you motivated and keep you positive..."</p><p>On the ice, Vlasic looks about the same as he did last season. He's still using his long reach to break up lots of passes and plays. He's still not physical whatsoever despite his 6-6 size; he entered Tuesday with only three hits credited to him.</p><p>His offensive contributions are limited, too, although he is taking charge to skate the puck out of the defensive zone more often. But his pairing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/22/blackhawks-breakouts-nhl-science-ian-cole-1000-games" >with Ian Cole</a> has arguably been the most reliable part of the Hawks' shaky defense.</p><p>Team-wise, Vlasic insists he has observed considerable improvement since the season began, even though "nothing is really going in" and translating to the scoreboard.</p><p>He also actually appreciates how difficult the Hawks' schedule has been. It has given them many opportunities to study how the league's best teams operate.</p><p>"It's fun, honestly, to play different teams that have had success — teams like Florida, Carolina and Vegas — that can give us an example of how they play," Vlasic said.</p><p>"After the first period [Sunday against Florida], we talked about how they do things in such a simple way. It's such a solid team game that they play. We came out in the second and third [periods] and tried to focus on adding that style of play to our game: simple, smart, working for each other. I felt like it was pretty effective."</p><p>The Hawks still ultimately <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/25/chicago-blackhawks-florida-panthers-ryan-donato-jeff-blashill-kevin-korchinski-patrick-kane-spencer-knight-ryan-greene" >lost</a> to the Panthers, of course. And there's a big difference between two periods of simple, smart, cohesive hockey and months upon months of it.</p><p>To climb out of this hole and back into the playoff race, the Hawks will need to somehow accomplish the latter, which is difficult to imagine. But there probably still is some speak-it-into-existence value in declaring it possible.</p>

entries.title: Bears DE Montez Sweat calls suspension 'devastating,' accepts that it stains his career and clouds his future
entries.summary: <p>Starting the day defensive end <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/04/bears-de-montez-sweat-out-to-reassert-himself-as-elite-pass-rusher-but-more-so-he-wants-to-finally-win" >Montez Sweat</a> arrived at Halas Hall, when <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> traded a second-round pick to make him a pillar of their future, he has been uneasy with the spotlight that comes with being the highest-paid player in the building.</p><p>So Tuesday likely was one of the most uncomfortable days of his career.</p><p>Sweat talked to reporters, at the urging of the team, for five minutes and was drenched from a post-practice workout as he addressed his two-game suspension for testing positive for performance-enhancing drugs. He’ll return Monday at the Seahawks.</p><p>Sweat declined to reveal details about when he tested positive or how something like that could happen to a professional athlete with a team of people helping manage what he puts in his body, but was open about how miserable the last two weeks have been.</p><p>He said it was “devastating” to be separated from the team during the Bears’ wins over the Falcons and Patriots and to stain his reputation.</p><p>“It's definitely something I’ve got to live with for my career,” Sweat said. “I never want to cheat the game, and I would never do it intentionally, but what happened happened and I'm moving forward.”</p><p>The path forward got cloudier after the suspension, though.</p><p>The biggest issue when it comes to Sweat’s future with the Bears is that he has been good, but not great. They traded not only a second-round pick (No. 40 overall in 2024), but also signed him to a four-year, $98 million deal.</p><p>In return, they’ve gotten 23 1/2 sacks over the equivalent of three seasons. If that number were doubled, this suspension would be merely a footnote for him and a relatively minor inconvenience for coach Ben Johnson and general manager Ryan Poles.</p><p>The suspension cost Sweat $2.3 million in pay, money that is credited back to the Bears’ salary-cap space, and invalidated any guarantees remaining in his contract. That makes it easier to trade him by the Nov. 10 deadline, though that’s highly unlikely.</p><p>What’s really in question for Sweat is whether he’ll be back next season.</p><p>Johnson said last season was Sweat’s best as a pro, including what he added as a run stopper as part of that opinion, but pass rushers are judged mainly by sacks. The best in the league don’t need anyone to talk about what they bring in run defense or how they’re creating pressure even if it doesn’t lead to sacks; those effects are assumed.</p><p>The Bears can move on from Sweat in the offseason for a negligible $4.1 million dead-cap hit rather than pay him $25.1 million. If they already were questioning whether they’ve been getting their money’s worth on his deal, a two-game suspension in the heart of the season doesn’t help.</p><p>“I take everything that comes with it,” Sweat said of how the suspension might affect his future with the team. “The only thing I can do now is just look forward and continue to play.”</p>

entries.title: Field-goal length, accuracy not on par with last year's 'massive leap'
entries.summary: <p>A new NFL rule last year pushed the revolution upon us.</p><p>Starting in 2025, teams were allowed to prepare their own kicking balls — special footballs used for kicks and punts — all throughout the game week. In the previous 25 years, teams could only do it on game day.</p><p>The result felt like the changing of the sport itself.</p><p>Kickers made more than half their tries of 60 yards or more last season. The Jaguars’ Cam Little set an NFL record by making a 68-yarder and later claimed second place by making a 67-yarder. Kickers went 12-for-22 from 60 yards or more — and 3-for-6 from 65 yards or more.</p><p>This year hasn’t pushed the edges of field goal range farther back, nor has it made kickers more accurate. Kickers have made 84.3% of their kicks this year, down from 85.6% the entirety of last year — and the weather hasn’t even turned nasty yet.</p><p>What’s remarkable, though, is from where kickers are missing. This year, players have made 79.5% of their tries from 40-49 yards. A year ago it was 84.3%.<br>The deep balls have been roughly the same — Kickers made a slightly higher percentage from 50-59 yards this year compared to last season, and slightly fewer from 60 yards and up.</p><p>That’s not the jump some projected after last season.</p><p>“The year before to last year, it was a massive leap,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> kicker Cairo Santos said Tuesday. “And now I think it’s the same.”</p><p>Everyone, though, seems to be trying, and making, kicks from the mid-50s.Almost two-thirds of the kickers in the league — 21 of the 33 who have made a kick this season — have a long of 56 yards or more this year. That includes Santos, who booted a career-high 58-yarder to salt away the Bears’ win against the Patriots on Thursday night.</p><p>Santos, who so upset about a previous miss that he couldn’t fully enjoy his late-game achievement Thursday night, said he grew to appreciate it over the weekend.</p><p>“I am happier,” he said. “It’s never as bad as you think and it’s never as good as you think either. I’m still mad, given how well I thought I kicked all week. There’s a lot to build on. Making that kick, the 58-longer, the confidence jumps even more.”</p><p>Kickers are more accurate from long range than ever before, thanks to factors such as year-round training all the way down to the youth level and the ability to kick inside domes and off artificial turf.</p><p>The “K-ball” rule change that began last year stands out the most, though. During the week, teams try to make the ball resemble a soccer ball as much as possible, trying to dull the points of the ball and make the leather softer. They can use the most basic of tools — water, towels, sponges and brushes — to remove a waxy coating. Teams can use ball for three games, maximum, and must have three balls at the ready for each game.</p><p>From 1960 to 2024, kickers made 49.9% of their kicks from 50 yards or more. Since the start of last year, kickers have made 68.6% of them.</p><p>While 2026 hasn’t continued the massive trajectory of 2025, Santos expects kicks to keep getting longer.</p><p>“I do think that you’re still going to start seeing bigger numbers — and a small increase,:” Santos said. “It’s gonna be 71, 72, 73 [yards].”</p>

entries.title: Walter Ousley, the first African American crew chief for Air Force One, dies at 81
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>As crew chief for Air Force One, South Side native Walter Ousley was responsible for maintaining and servicing the aircraft during the administration of former President Richard M. Nixon.</p><p>"He was first African American to serve in that role," said his son, Peter Ousley.</p><p>"He always said that despite how Nixon was perceived after his presidency, he was someone who treated the crew and people around him with respect, and it was an honor for him to shake his hand and serve the president," Peter Ousley said.</p><p>After graduating from Tilden High School in 1964, Mr. Ousley joined the Air Force and learned the mechanical and electrical systems of aircraft.</p><p>While serving in Vietnam, he once used chewing gum to improvise a fix to a leaky engine — while the aircraft was briefly on the ground in hostile territory. </p><p>When he was tapped for duty on Air Force One, family members, including his grandmother, were called during routine security screenings, since the position required top-secret clearance.</p><p>"His grandma received a call and then quickly reached out to Mr. Ousley with concern: 'What did you do? There's all these people asking all these questions about you,'" Peter Ousley said.</p><p>After being discharged from the military, Mr. Ousley earned a bachelor’s degree from the University of Maryland and a graduate degree from Roosevelt University.</p><p>In 1973, he began working for Catholic Charities of the Archdiocese of Chicago, finishing his 35-year career there in 2008 as chief entries.title: Bulls have serious 'right-now' issues to deal with as schedule toughens
entries.summary: <p>BOSTON – The Xs and Os will happen.</p><p>Bulls veteran Norman Powell has been around the game long enough to know that a new team, especially a young team, has to go through some growing pains to figure that part of the game out.</p><p>That’s just the reality of life in the Association.</p><p>But the “right-now things,” as Powell calls them, well, they need to be figured out right now.</p><p>Rebounding, defending and physicality are all ongoing issues for the 1-3 Bulls, and enough so that Powell discusses them daily with the group or individual teammates. Leadership 101 where he has no problem playing the role of professor.</p><p>"The timeline needs to be next game," Powell said. "It’s no, 'Oh, we’ve got to figure out how to rebound.' That’s just effort, effort and attention to detail, and competitiveness. My timeline is 10-15 games in on how we’re going to play, but the little things like effort and things we can control? That is a right-now thing. The Xs and Os of execution offensively and how we’re going to play on that end, that takes time. But the effort and attention to detail, how we’re going to guard? That’s something that happens immediately.”</p><p>Something that hasn’t happened enough.</p><p>The Bulls were out-manned in the season-opening loss in Toronto, then showed some fight in the win in Milwaukee. But the last two games, against Washington and Boston, had too many let-go-of-the-rope moments, starting with poor play out of the halftime locker room and into the third quarter.</p><p>At least against the Wizards they fought back in the fourth quarter to make the game competitive. Not the case in Boston on Monday, where the Celtics started throwing body blows to start the third and achieved the knockout shortly after, outscoring the Bulls 39-21 and never looking back.</p><p>“I think we start games alright,” guard Josh Giddey said. “It’s just the third quarter that’s kind of killing us and what we’ve got to get better at. It’s been a couple games now that the first unit has started off slow and then we’re relying on our second unit to pick us back up, so it starts with us. If you look at it from a game perspective, that’s probably an issue but there are a lot of things beneath that, that we need to clean up if we want to be competitive. I’ve got to be way better, we’ve got to figure it out together.”</p><p>Which is what Powell was signed on to try and do — help the group figure out how to deal with obstacles that a rebuild presents.</p><p>“I’m going to continue to stay on them, continue to talk about what I see,” Powell said of his role as veteran leader. “I’m still learning each and every one of them, but I see something, talk to them as a collective, talk to guys individually of how we can be better.</p><p>“A lot of games are lost in the third quarter. You’ve got to come out (from halftime) with the right mindset, pay attention to detail, the same aggressiveness offensively and defensively as a collective. It’s not one person, but just collectively we’ve got to be better.”</p><p>That’s because Powell knows what’s coming. A Wednesday home meeting with the defending champion Knicks, then a three-game road trip back to Boston, off to Philadelphia, and then to the Knicks again.</p><p>The effort parts of the game, specifically rebounding and physicality, will not be optional in Powell’s world.</p><p>“We’ve talked about it,” he added. “It’s something we’ve got to understand and pick up because I told them with these games coming up, we can be on the outside looking in really quickly and we’ve got to fix that effort on that side of the ball.”</p>

entries.title: Bears practice report: RB Kyle Monangai still out
entries.summary: <p>What happened Tuesday at Halas Hall:</p><h3>Monangai out, Scott up </h3><p>Kyle Monangai, who is battling a toe injury, was not present at the portion of Tuesday's walk-through that was open to the media.</p><p>Minutes before practice began, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> promoted another running back, Zavier Scott, from the practice squad. Scott had appeared in three games via a standard game day elevation, the maximum number any team can do that without signing a player to the 53-man roster. Scott is not a Monangai replacement, however; he's yet to play an offensive snap this season but has played 46 special teams snaps, forcing one fumble and making five tackles.</p><p>The Bears don't have to file an injury report until Thursday.</p><h3>Seahawks get help</h3><p>The Seahawks — the Bears' opponent Monday night — made the first big trade of the season, sending a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-rounder to the Colts for eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quentin Nelson. Nelson is in the last year of his contract. Interim general manager Ed Dodds figures to keep selling, with defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and running back Jonathan Taylor among the most attractive pieces on the roster. The NFL's trade deadline is in two weeks.</p><h3><b>Others out</b></h3><p>Rookie Malik Muhammad, who left Thursday night's win against the Patriots because of his own toe injury, did not practice Tuesday. Neither did fellow cornerback Tyrique Stevenson, who has dealt with various injuries since the start of training camp. The Bears were without cornerback Nick McCloud, too — they cut him to make room for Scott.<br></p>

entries.title: Police seek gunman who shot 2 men inside Loop 7-Eleven
entries.summary: <p>Detectives are searching for a gunman who burst into a Loop 7-Eleven Monday night and shot two men, according to Chicago police and a witness.</p><p>The attack unfolded at 9:45 p.m. at the 7-Eleven at Adams Street and Wabash Avenue. </p><p>"We saw a bunch of cop cars pulling up," said Lou D., manager of nearby Princess Nails at 25 E. Adams St.</p><p>Two men inside the business, 26 and 23, were shot after a brief altercation between the gunman and the 26-year-old, police said. The shooter ran away and was not in custody. </p><p>The 26-year-old and the 23-year-old were taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in fair condition. The older man suffered multiple gunshot wounds, while the other man's foot was grazed by a bullet, police said. </p><p>Area 3 detectives are investigating.</p>
