entries.title: CTA board approves $40 million in accessibility renovations to California Blue Line station
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Transit Authority board voted to approve construction contracts for a revitalization project at the California Blue Line station site. </p><p>The work — paid for by state transportation and local TIF funds — is set to begin in late fall 2027, according to the CTA.</p><p>The project will expand platforms and canopies and add two elevators, new stairs and accessible doors at the site. General infrastructure improvements such as lighting, sidewalks, ramps, drainage, and landscaping will also be done.</p><p>The California station, which the CTA said saw 1.1 million commuters in 2025, <u>last underwent work</u> in 2014 as part of the city's Your New Blue Project. At the time, it received new lighting, signage, refurbished walls, stairs, platforms and bicycle racks.</p><p>A temporary stationhouse and entrance will be built at St. George’s Court to be used while construction is ongoing.</p><p>The agency said it is part of its ongoing All Stations Accessibility Program, which aims to make all rail stations fully accessible by 2038.</p><p>“An accessible CTA gives more people the freedom to travel independently and connects them to everything our region has to offer,” CTA interim President Nora Leerhsen said in a statement. “This investment will bring that promise to life at the California Blue Line station, delivering a modern, welcoming station that better serves riders with disabilities and the entire community."</p>

entries.summary: <p>Police are searching for a man who reportedly attempted to sexually assault an 11-year-old girl en route to school in the Garfield Park neighborhood Tuesday morning, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The girl was walking in the 3900 block of West Washington Boulevard at 8:30 a.m. when she was approached by a man who attempted to sexually assault her before fleeing the area on foot.</p><p>Police did not provide a description of the suspect. </p>

entries.title: Student faces possible charges over social media post that suggested threat at South Side high school.
entries.summary: <p>Charges are pending for a teen girl whose social media post referencing explosives prompted a visit by Chicago police officers to her high school in the Kenwood area Tuesday morning.</p><p>At 9:09 a.m., those officers recovered fireworks from the 15-year-old, who allegedly said on social media she had explosives at Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. College Preparatory High School, 4445 S. Drexel Blvd., police said.</p><p>The school, which has nearly 1,000 students, was later declared clear of explosives, and police later found more unused fireworks, allegedly belonging to the teen, in the 600 block of East 51st Street.</p><p>Charges are pending, police said.</p><p>In a statement, Brian Kelly, the school's principal, said the school received a threat on social media and contacted police and the Chicago Public Schools Office of Safety and Security.</p><p>“We take all potential threats extremely seriously,” said Kelly. “The investigation is complete, and CPD has deemed the potential threat as non-credible. There is no safety threat to our school, and all of our students and staff members are safe.”</p>

entries.title: Courting death by hauling top-heavy wooden floats in Japan — just another risky guy thing
entries.summary: <p>The news is flushing out my siblings lately.</p><p>Just as my sister Debbie showed up in Chicago, Pope Leo XIV went under the knife for lung cancer. Deb has been kicking cancer's ass for years, so <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/10/15/open-letter-pope-leo-xiv-lung-cancer-steinberg" target="_blank" >tapping her wisdom</a> seemed a no-brainer.</p><p>Several readers replied, "You have a sister?" Well, I'm supposed to be writing a column for a Chicago newspaper, not a chatty meet-the-family Christmas letter.</p><p>And yet. News has a will of its own.</p><p>Now it's my younger brother's turn. Sam is no stranger to readers, particularly of my books. It is he who bails me out of jail in "Drunkard." He's also a plot point in "You Were Never in Chicago," as I trace the classic newcomer's path of coming here, getting a job, then bringing family to Chicago and helping them get jobs. I rented an apartment with a spare bedroom on Logan Boulevard, and enticed him to move here from Tokyo, where his apartment was so small I could span its width with my arms spread and one foot planted on the floor. And I have short arms.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e80000" name="module-e80000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Sam still has the Big Love for Japan, and goes back often. He and his wife Yuri were there when my sister showed up, which would have not been the stuff of a column, except for one reason he went — to participate in the <i>Danjiri Matsuri</i> — an annual fall festival where huge wooden floats are maneuvered through the streets by acolytes wearing cotton happi coats.</p><p>I knew it was dangerous — the festival i<i>s</i> sort of a Japanese running of the bulls at Pamplona: a chance to party in the street, risk being killed, and survive. I thought of telling him, "Don't get crushed." But that seemed a prissy, older brother concern. </p><p>What I said instead was, "I want to see a picture." Because he can fall down in that department. I would have left it at that. Then two participants were crushed to death in Osaka, and 16 injured. <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/19/world/asia/danjiri-festival-deaths-osaka-japan.html" target="_blank" >The New York Times</a> found four others who died in 2022 and 2023. Suddenly, I was sitting on a big international news story, so designated Sam as a Sun-Times foreign correspondent and got to work.</p><p>Weren't you worried about being killed?</p><p>"Obviously, there is some trepidation regarding that," Sam said. "It's not lost on us that this is a dangerous event, that people get hurt all the time. After your shoulder injury, I [worried] I'm going to be next."</p><p>Those carrying the floats chant, <i>"</i><i>Yoisho, ja!</i>"<b> </b>— basically, "Heave ho!" "Very very big. This one is more like 40 or 50 people. You have five or six different shrines going around at any one time. It was interesting. They told everyone to bring a towel and put it under their happi coat, so you don't wreck your shoulder. Everyone is given a number. Very Japanese, very efficient. You stand by your number and go lift it up once, then put it back down. Starting slow. You do a couple laps around the shrine, lifting the shrine higher above your head, shaking it, bringing it back down."</p><p>I assumed it is a well-lubricated undertaking.</p><p>"There's a little bit of that," said my brother, who had a single beer beforehand. "Alcohol is definitely part of the equation. Also part of why it becomes more dangerous."</p><p>And what are you thinking during this?</p><p>"My main thought was: 'I don't want this coming down on my shoulder.' On average, I'm pretty tall, compared to most people there. The way the physics of the turn works, a lot of weight starts to fulcrum. It's not that long-lasting, but you do have that point where you feel like, 'God, this is a lot of weight.'"</p><p>I'm not sure I'd go to the corner of Shermer and Walters to participate. What made it worth flying to Japan to do?</p><p>"I like the whole idea of doing a testosterone-laden guy thing," Sam said. "There's not a lot of opportunity to do that kind of stuff in the United States."</p><p>The takeaway: It was fun; he didn't die.</p><p>"It was a very cool experience," he said. "I'm ready to go back and do it again next year."</p><p>Somehow, that reasoning was surprisingly persuasive. A decade ago we took the <i>shinkansen</i> — the bullet train — together across Japan, to Kumamoto, to attend <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/7/28/18406926/steinberg-a-break-from-politics-sort-of-with-japan-s-top-bear" target="_blank" >the birthday party </a>of a teddy bear. This struck me as a similarly worthy event.</p><p>"Maybe I will go with you," I said. Because really, how often do you get the chance?</p>

entries.title: Suben las tasas de graduación y de ingreso a la universidad en CPS, pero muchos batallan para terminar
entries.summary: <p>Los estudiantes de las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS) están obteniendo cada vez más créditos universitarios mientras aún cursan la secundaria y se gradúan e inscriben en la universidad en porcentajes más altos que en el pasado, pero muchos aún tienen dificultades para terminar la universidad y obtener un título.</p><p>Esas son algunas de las conclusiones de un <a class="Link" href="https://toandthrough.uchicago.edu/tool/cps/pai/2025/#" target="_blank" >informe publicado</a> por el Proyecto To&Through y el Consorcio de Investigación Escolar de la Universidad de Chicago, junto con datos del distrito publicados la semana pasada.</p><p>El informe halló que el 56% de los estudiantes de CPS que se graduaron en la generación de 2019 e ingresaron de inmediato a una universidad de cuatro años obtuvieron su título o un certificado laboral dentro de seis años, mientras que el 32% de quienes comenzaron de inmediato en una universidad de dos años alcanzaron un título o certificado en el mismo periodo. Esos porcentajes apenas se han movido en cuatro años.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b50000" name="module-b50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En general, sólo el 48% de los graduados de CPS de 2019 que se matricularon de inmediato en la universidad obtuvo un título o certificado en seis años, señaló el informe —muy por debajo de la tasa nacional del 64%.</p><p>Al mismo tiempo, los estudiantes de CPS se gradúan e ingresan a la universidad a tasas cercanas o en los niveles más altos de la historia. La tasa de graduación de CPS aumentó a 82.6% para la clase de 2025, y volvió a subir para la clase de 2026 hasta 83.4%, dijeron funcionarios del distrito.</p><p>Mientras tanto, el 67% de la generación de 2025 se inscribió de inmediato en la universidad, frente al 58% de hace una década y por encima del promedio nacional, según el informe.</p><p>Los datos indican que, aunque más estudiantes de secundaria están alcanzando el siguiente nivel educativo, muchos aún necesitan recursos y apoyo adicionales una vez que llegan allí.</p><p>Pero Dominique McKoy, director ejecutivo del Proyecto To&Through, añadió que también muestra cuánto han crecido las tasas de graduación en las últimas décadas.</p><p>"Tenemos que recordar que, en la memoria reciente, este era un distrito que tenía una tasa de graduación de la secundaria del 50%", dijo McKoy. "Teníamos algunas zonas comunitarias en la Ciudad de Chicago con tasas de graduación de secundaria del 25%".</p><p>El informe también encontró persistentes disparidades raciales y de género en las tasas de finalización universitaria.</p><p>Entre los graduados de CPS de 2019, los hombres jóvenes tenían muchas menos probabilidades de graduarse con un título universitario en seis años que las mujeres jóvenes —un patrón que se mantuvo en todos los grupos raciales y étnicos, según el informe.</p><p>La disparidad fue especialmente marcada entre los hombres jóvenes negros y latinos, de los cuales menos de un tercio se graduaron con una licenciatura en seis años.</p><p>Las mujeres latinas, los estudiantes asiáticos e isleños del Pacífico y los estudiantes blancos anglosajones de la generación de 2019 completaron un título o certificado en porcentajes más altos, según el informe.</p><p>McKoy dijo que los datos ofrecen "probablemente algunas de las pruebas más contundentes sobre la necesidad de iniciativas" como el Plan de Éxito para Estudiantes Negros de CPS (Black Student Success Plan), que busca reducir las brechas académicas entre los estudiantes negros.</p><p>El informe señala que los estudiantes que comenzaron la universidad en 2019 y quienes se graduaron de la secundaria en 2025 atravesaron hechos importantes que afectaron su escolaridad, como la pandemia de COVID-19 y la campaña masiva de deportaciones de la administración de Trump el año pasado.</p><p>Aun así, las tasas generales de finalización universitaria entre los estudiantes de CPS han aumentado lentamente con el tiempo.</p><p>El porcentaje de graduados de CPS que se matricularon en una universidad de cuatro años y completaron algún tipo de título dentro de seis años aumentó de alrededor del 53% a casi el 56% entre la generación de 2010 y la de 2019. Y ese incremento fue aún mayor para quienes se inscribieron en colegios de dos años.</p><p>La tasa de graduación del distrito ha aumentado de manera sostenida en las últimas dos décadas. En 2000, menos de la mitad de los estudiantes de CPS se graduaban en cuatro años, muestran los datos del distrito. CPS alcanzó su tasa de graduación más alta en 2023, cuando casi el 85% de los estudiantes obtuvo su diploma a tiempo, según el informe del Proyecto To&Through y la Universidad de Chicago.</p><p>Estos estudiantes también están obteniendo créditos universitarios y certificaciones laborales durante sus años de escuela secundaria a una tasa más alta. Más del 57% de los graduados de CPS de la generación de 2026 obtuvieron créditos universitarios y certificados profesionales, 10 puntos porcentuales más que hace cuatro años, según datos del distrito escolar publicados esta semana.</p><p>Eso incluye certificaciones técnicas en oficios especializados, créditos por cursos de Advanced Placement y el sello de biliteracidad, un reconocimiento que acredita el dominio del inglés y otro idioma y que puede otorgar créditos universitarios.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Pritzker's PAC is spending to back Dems in heated Kansas, Mississippi Senate races
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker's Ready for the Fight PAC is sending $1.5 million to help Democrats win the Senate in Mississippi and Kansas — part of more than $40 million in spending the billionaire governor is doling out in the midterm elections and to Democratic causes to try to boost anti-Trump candidates and help Democrats win the House and Senate.</p><p>Pritzker is honorary chair of the PAC, which was launched in September and vowed to spend $15 million to help Democrats in districts that President Donald Trump had previously won. </p><p>Republicans have a 53-47 majority in the Senate, and 35 seats are up for election. Democrats must hold all of their seats and flip four GOP seats to take the Senate. In the House, Republicans have a 218-214 majority with all 435 seats up for election (including some currently vacant seats). </p><p>The latest investments include a $1 million ad buy in the Mississippi U.S. Senate race, where Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, faces Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, who blocked Colom's nomination to be a federal judge during the Biden administration. In a sign the race is competitive, Trump on Monday held a rally in Corinth, Mississippi, to support Hyde-Smith. Polls conducted in August and October by Democratic pollsters showed Colom with a slight lead in a state that has the largest proportion of Black voters in the country. </p><p>The Associated Press reported Colom attended Trump's rally to listen to what was on GOP supporters' minds. </p><p>“I’m here because Cindy’s doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can’t take a chance,” Trump said at the rally. </p><p>The PAC is also spending $500,000 in the Kansas U.S. Senate race, where Democrat Adam Hamilton faces incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. Polls are also showing the race is neck-and-neck. </p><p>Trump is also holding a rally Saturday in Salina, Kansas, marking his second visit to the state in less than two weeks.</p><p>The Ready for the Fight PAC is also funding voter mobilization efforts in Mississippi and South Carolina to help boost Democratic turnout and help candidates up and down the ballot. </p><p>The PAC said it's investing in races that "national Democrats have historically overlooked." The latest spends follow the PAC's advertising efforts targeting MAGA Republicans across the country, including House races in Texas, Arkansas, Alabama, New Mexico and Ohio. </p><p>Since 2025, Pritzker has given at least $40 million to Democrats and allied causes — including campaigns for the U.S. House and Senate, attorney general, secretary of state, county judges and state parties in more than a dozen states, as well as ballot fights over abortion rights and redistricting. That figure includes $15 million he contributed to Ready for the Fight.</p><p>Some of Pritzker’s largest contributions this cycle include $1.5 million to the Wisconsin Democratic Party; $1.2 million to Gina Hinojosa’s campaign for Texas governor; and $1 million each to the Democratic Governors Association, Senate Majority PAC, Ohio Democratic Party, the House Majority PAC and Project Battleground, a leadership committee helping Keisha Lance Bottoms’ Georgia gubernatorial campaign. He also gave $310,000 to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.</p><p>Pritzker has spent more than $90.5 million to support his own reelection campaign for his third term. In total, Pritzker has given himself more than $439 million to support his three bids for governor. Forbes estimates Pritzker's wealth at $4.2 billion. </p>
